overview: UDP sends individual messages without a transport handshake. It preserves datagram boundaries but leaves recovery, ordering and timing decisions to the application.
outro: Voice frames left without a transport handshake. One datagram was lost, but subsequent frames continued on schedule. RTP supplied ordering and timing information, while the application chose how to handle the missing audio.
steps: The first voice frame can leave immediately. UDP adds source and destination ports, a length and a checksum, without establishing a TCP-style connection.
The sender encodes small pieces of audio into separate datagrams. RTP sequence numbers and timestamps describe their order and playback timing. UDP itself does not interpret those media fields.
One datagram fails to reach the receiver. UDP has no automatic retransmission, so the next voice frame continues on schedule. The receiver notices the gap through the RTP sequence number.
The remote endpoint sends voice frames back to the client’s port. These are independent messages rather than TCP acknowledgments. The application manages the two media streams.

A voice application may conceal the missing sound rather than wait for a late retransmission. A different UDP application could implement its own reliable delivery. UDP leaves that policy above the transport layer.
